name: Octopus Back Take
keyCorrections: If you can't take the back, your far hip wrap is too loose — tighten the wrap before spinning.
If they face you during the spin, you spun too wide — keep the spin tight to their body.
If they sprawl on the spin, you spun too early — wait for them to fully commit the post.
description: Use the octopus guard hip angle to expose the back when the opponent posts against the sweep — transitioning from a failed sweep into back control.
shortInstruction: They post against the sweep? Spin under and take the back — their defense becomes your entry.
summary: The octopus back take is the highest percentage follow-up to the octopus guard sweep. When you attempt the octopus sweep (pulling their far hip across your body), many opponents will respond by posting a hand or stepping to defend. This reaction creates the exact angle you need to spin under their arm, circle behind them, and take the back. The octopus back take transforms a defended sweep into the most dominant position in BJJ.
whyItWorks: When they post a hand to defend the sweep, that arm is committed and cannot block your spin entry.
The octopus guard already has you at the perfect angle for the back take — you are already sitting to their side.
The far hip wrap gives you the pivot point for the spin — you rotate around their center of gravity.
Danaher principle: the sweep and back take form a dilemma — defend the sweep, lose the back; defend the back, lose the sweep.
commonMistakes: Spinning before they post — you need their post to clear your path to the back.
Losing the far hip wrap during the spin — the wrap is your steering wheel for the back take.
Spinning the wrong direction — you spin under their posted arm, not around their body.
Not securing the seatbelt quickly enough after the spin — they will turn to face you.
coachingCues: Sweep bait, post reaction, spin under, back taken.
Their post is your entry — if they don't post, you sweep.
Spin under the arm, not around the body.
Seatbelt first, hooks second — don't rush the sequence.
safetySummary: Keep your head protected during the spin — your head goes under their armpit, not into their elbow.
Do not spin if they have a grip on your collar or neck — strip the grip first.
When landing on the back, protect your own knees from landing awkwardly.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Octopus guard: sweep attempt → opponent posts → spin under their arm → take the back → seatbelt → hooks → attack.

decisionTree.condition: The octopus back take works in one movement: sweep post
they don't post (defend the sweep by sitting back)
decisionTree.action: continue with the sweep — the back take is only when they post.

moneyDetails: The far hip wrap must be maintained throughout the spin — it is your control point.
Spin under their posted arm — your head should pass under their armpit, not around their body.
As you spin, release the leg control and re-establish with your hooks behind their thighs.
Once behind, lock the seatbelt immediately — seatbelt before hooks.
nextStep: After the octopus back take, learn back control and the back attack system.
fixItFast: Can't spin under? Your far hip wrap is too loose — tighten it.
They face you? Spin tighter to their body — your path is too wide.
They sprawl? You spun too early — wait for the full post commitment.
